title: Staking up
subtitle: How to stake up a woven willow basket base and lock the upsett
excerpt: Staking up is the step between finishing a basket base and starting the sides: inserting side stakes into the base weave and bending them upright with a locked upsett row. Done correctly, the stakes are evenly spaced, at a consistent angle, and locked firmly enough that the weaving cannot displace them. Done wrong, the sides are uneven or the stakes pull free during weaving.
sourceNotes: Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the staking up and upsett sequence; Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the side-stake insertion method.

glossaryTerms.definition: The first waling rows worked after staking up, which physically bend the side stakes upright and lock them at the base.
A weaving pattern using multiple rods that chase each other around the basket, creating a strong structural row.
A pointed metal tool for opening gaps in the base weave to allow the side stake to be inserted.
Willow boiled to fix a tan colour and stripped of bark. The standard material for traditional English willow baskets.

content.text: Staking up is the hinge between the base and the sides of any woven willow basket. Every basket in this sub-category that has upright sides uses this technique. The sequence is: trim the base, insert side stakes, kink the stakes at the base, work the
upsett
wale. Each step has specific things that go wrong if rushed, this guide covers all of them.
When to use this technique
After completing any woven willow base, before starting the sides. Applies to all round, oval, and square-base basket forms.
What you need
Side stakes in
buff willow

(or green willow). The stakes should be at least twice the intended side height, to allow for the length buried in the base weave. Cut the butt (thick) end of each stake to a point before insertion. The
bodkin
is used to open the base weave for the stake insertion.
Inserting the stakes

Use the bodkin to open a gap in the base weave directly alongside each base stick, not between base sticks, but right alongside. Push the bodkin in at a slight upward angle to open the weave without breaking the base rod. Insert the side stake into the gap, pointed end first, and push it at least 7 cm into the base. The stake should sit firmly with hand pressure; if it pulls out easily, the gap was too wide and needs to be tightened with a narrow shim of willow alongside the stake.
Kinked upright

Once all stakes are inserted, each stake must be kinked at the base to allow it to bend upright without snapping. Use your thumbnail to press a sharp kink into the stake right at the base weave surface, the kink allows the stake to pivot up to vertical without the fibres breaking. In buff willow, a firm kink holds; in brittle seasoned willow, you may need to grip the stake and gently rotate as you bend. Tie all the kinked stakes together loosely at the top with a piece of string to keep them vertical during the upsett.
The upsett
Work three rounds of four-rod
wale

directly at the base of the stakes. Four-rod wale: start four weavers at consecutive stakes; each weaver passes in front of two stakes, behind one, and out. The four weavers chase each other around the basket. The upsett wale physically bends the stakes upright with its own tension, after three rounds, the stakes stand vertically without the string tie.
Checking the upsett
All stakes are vertical when viewed from the side.
Stake spacing is even all the way around.
No stake wobbles when pressed from the side.
The base still lies flat after the upsett rows.

attrs.symptom: Stakes lean outward during the upsett and won't stay vertical
attrs.cause: The upsett wale tension is not strong enough to pull them inward, or the base weave is too loose to anchor the stake butts
attrs.fix: Work the upsett wale with more tension on the weavers, each weaver should be pulled snug before the next pass begins. If the base weave is loose, add a packing weave row directly at the base between the stakes before working the upsett.

attrs.symptom: A stake splits when kinked upright
attrs.cause: The kink was made at too blunt an angle; the fibres buckled rather than bending
attrs.fix: Dampen the stake at the kink point with water and re-bend slowly. If it has split, remove the stake, pare the split end clean with secateurs, and re-insert a replacement alongside.
